The Education

Why Internal Medicine Billing Requires Three Separate Specializations at Once

Outpatient E/M complexity, inpatient status determination, and chronic care program management each require distinct billing expertise. Most billing teams handle one well and miss the other two entirely.

Internal medicine billing is the process of coding and submitting insurance claims for the full spectrum of comprehensive adult medicine from complex outpatient E/M visits managing multiple chronic conditions, to hospital medicine, observation care, critical care, care coordination programs, and preventive services. The billing complexity of internal medicine is threefold: it demands the deepest E/M coding expertise in ambulatory medicine, the most compliance-sensitive inpatient status decisions in hospital billing, and the most revenue-dense chronic care management programs in primary care.

The 2021 AMA E/M revisions directly reward the cognitive work that internists perform better than any prior coding framework. Medical decision-making complexity the number and severity of problems managed, the data reviewed, and the risk of complications maps directly to the multi-system complexity that defines internal medicine practice. An internist managing a patient with diabetes, CKD stage 3, hypertension, heart failure, GERD, depression, hyperlipidemia, and a new complaint of exertional dyspnea is providing a level 5 visit (99215) by clinical definition. Yet that same visit is coded at 99213 by practices that default to conservative coding. PMEx reads the note and codes to the level it actually supports.

The hospital medicine environment adds a second billing complexity that does not exist in outpatient internal medicine: the observation versus inpatient status determination. Medicare's Two-Midnight Rule states that a patient expected to require hospital care spanning at least two midnights generally meets criteria for inpatient admission. Short stays under two midnights are typically observation status. Coding an observation patient as inpatient admission creates Medicare Part A claim denial and audit risk. Coding a patient who meets inpatient criteria as observation results in lower Part B reimbursement and significantly higher out-of-pocket cost for the patient.

The third environment chronic care management represents the largest untapped revenue stream in internal medicine. Internists managing panels of 500 to 2,000 patients commonly have 200 to 600 patients qualifying for CCM (99490), 20 to 100 patients qualifying for Principal Care Management (99424/99425) for single high-complexity conditions, and 15 to 40 monthly discharges qualifying for TCM (99495/99496). None of these programs require additional appointments. They require a billing team that tracks them, documents them, and submits them consistently every month.

The combined internal medicine revenue opportunity: E/M level correction from 74% to 97% accuracy, CCM and PCM program launch, TCM episode capture, ACP coding, and prolonged services identification adds $100,000 to $200,000 annually to a 3-provider internal medicine practice from existing patients, existing visits, existing documentation.

The Most Dangerous Billing Decision in Hospital Medicine

The Observation vs. Inpatient Status Trap

Medicare's Two-Midnight Rule determines whether a hospital patient is billed as inpatient (Part A) or observation (Part B). A patient whose physician expects to require hospital care spanning at least two midnights generally qualifies for inpatient admission. A patient not expected to span two midnights is observation. The rule sounds simple. In practice, it is one of the most judgment-intensive and compliance-sensitive determinations in U.S. hospital billing.

Getting it wrong in either direction is expensive. Billing a patient as inpatient when they do not meet the Two-Midnight Rule criteria and Medicare's MAC denies the claim in a Targeted Probe and Educate review results in full claim recoupment and potential systemic audit exposure if the pattern is widespread. Billing a patient as observation when they clearly meet inpatient criteria results in Part B reimbursement at a significantly lower rate, and the patient faces substantially higher cost-sharing under observation status (outpatient copays rather than inpatient deductible structure).

PMEx applies CMS Two-Midnight Rule criteria to every hospital admission decision reviewing the clinical documentation for expected length of stay, medical necessity justification for the admission level, and the attending physician's expectation at the time of admission. We code the admission correctly the first time, eliminating both the compliance risk of inpatient overcoding and the revenue risk of observation undercoding.

INPATIENT Part A

When Inpatient Is Correct and How to Document It

Inpatient admission is appropriate when the physician expects the patient to require hospital care spanning at least two midnights. The decision must be based on documented clinical factors at the time of admission not retrospectively. PMEx reviews admitting physician notes for Two-Midnight Rule supporting language and flags documentation gaps before the claim is submitted.

OBSERVATION Part B

When Observation Is Correct and What Changes for Billing

Observation status patients are outpatients receiving observation services. Physician billing uses hospital E/M codes with POS 22 for outpatient hospital, not POS 21 inpatient. Observation same-day discharge uses 99234/99235/99236. Getting the POS code wrong denies the claim regardless of the clinical accuracy of the admission decision.

COMPLIANCE RISK

The CMS Targeted Probe and Educate (TPE) Audit Risk

CMS MACs actively audit short inpatient stays under the TPE program specifically targeting providers whose inpatient billing patterns show a high rate of stays under two midnights. Practices billing observation patients as inpatient create systematic audit exposure. PMEx creates compliance-ready documentation for every hospital admission before the claim is submitted.

Inpatient Status Denial

Medicare MAC Denies Inpatient Claim Two-Midnight Rule Not Met

Hospitalist admits a patient in observation who does not clearly meet the Two-Midnight Rule expectation. Claim submitted as inpatient Part A. MAC reviews, determines observation was appropriate, and denies the Part A claim. Recoupment request issued. Similar pattern found across multiple admissions in the same review period.

PMEx reviews every hospital admission against Two-Midnight Rule criteria before the inpatient claim is submitted. The admitting note is checked for documentation of the physician's expectation regarding care spanning two midnights. Claims not meeting the standard are routed to observation billing with correct POS and code set before submission.

CCM Documentation Denial

Payer Audits and Denies CCM Claims Time Log Insufficient

Internal medicine practice submits 99490 for 250 enrolled CCM patients. Aetna selects 18 for documentation review. Monthly time logs are missing for 7, the care coordinator notes are incomplete for another 4, and 3 care plans have not been updated since enrollment. 14 claims denied simultaneously during audit review.

PMEx maintains monthly CCM time logs, care plan update records, and care coordinator notes for every enrolled patient in a payer-audit-ready format. Every CCM claim is submitted with a complete monthly documentation record. No CCM audit results in denial for documentation insufficiency on any PMEx-managed internal medicine program.

Split/Shared Visit Error

Hospital APP + Attending Visit Denied for Incorrect Modifier

Internal medicine attending and NP both see the inpatient on the same day. One claim submitted without Modifier FS (split/shared visit). Or both submit claims independently payer denies one as duplicate of the other. Split/shared hospital visit billing is among the most frequently miscoded in hospital medicine, per AAPC.

PMEx applies Modifier FS on all split/shared inpatient encounters, routes the claim under the provider who performed the substantive portion of the visit (in 2023 the MDM-based substantive standard applies), and prevents duplicate billing from multiple provider submissions on the same patient on the same date of service.

Medical Necessity Denial

Extended Inpatient Stay Denied CMS Criteria Not Documented

Patient hospitalized 5 days. Commercial payer uses InterQual criteria for concurrent review authorization. Attending notes day 3 onward do not document specific InterQual criteria supporting continued stay. Payer denies days 3 through 5 retroactively $3,600 to $5,400 in hospital day charges uncollected per patient, per episode.

PMEx reviews attending notes against InterQual and MCG criteria for extended stay concurrent review before authorization renewals are submitted. Clinical documentation gaps are flagged and supplemented with attending review before the claim goes out. Zero concurrent review denials on PMEx-managed internal medicine inpatient programs.

Prior Auth Gap

Specialty Medication or Advanced Test Ordered Without Authorization

Internist orders a PET scan, a specialty biologic, or a cardiac MRI for a high-complexity patient. Claim submitted after the service is completed. Payer reviews and denies for prior authorization not obtained before the service date. The patient has already been treated. The practice has no leverage. The claim goes uncollected.

PMEx Prior Auth submits authorization requests for all high-value diagnostic tests and specialty medications with clinical documentation from your EHR before the service date. U.S. Internal Medicine Billing in 2025

Internal medicine practices manage the highest chronic disease burden per physician in U.S. ambulatory care yet consistently collect significantly below the revenue their clinical complexity warrants. The gap is not from payer behavior. It is from billing infrastructure that does not match the complexity of what internists actually do.

The 2021 AMA E/M revisions were specifically designed to reward the cognitive work internal medicine physicians perform. Medical decision complexity the framework that replaced multi-component history and exam maps precisely to the multi-system chronic disease management that defines internal medicine practice. Practices that implemented 2021 documentation correctly saw immediate E/M revenue increases. Those that did not and most did not are still leaving that revenue on the table every day.

The denial environment has intensified on the inpatient side. CMS's Targeted Probe and Educate program is specifically scrutinizing short inpatient stays at hospitalist programs across the country. Practices with systematic observation-to-inpatient overcoding are receiving MAC demand letters for recoupment. PMEx manages hospital status determination as a compliance function not just a billing function protecting practices from audit risk while maximizing correct inpatient revenue where it is warranted.

Common Questions

Internal Medicine Billing Answered

PMEx coders evaluate every encounter against 2021 AMA E/M complexity criteria reviewing problem count and severity, data reviewed (labs, imaging, records, tests ordered), and risk of complications (prescription drug management, hospitalization risk). For internists managing multiple chronic conditions, most established patient visits qualify as level 4 (99214) or level 5 (99215) yet many practices code 60 to 70 percent as level 3. PMEx corrects this systematically from the first claim, increasing revenue per visit without changing any clinical documentation requirements.

Yes. PMEx manages hospital initial care (99221 through 99223), subsequent care (99231 through 99233), and discharge day (99238 through 99239) billing for hospitalists and internal medicine physicians with inpatient responsibilities. We apply correct medical decision complexity criteria for hospital E/M levels and manage split and shared visit billing when APPs are involved applying Modifier FS on the claim for the provider who performed the substantive portion of the visit, as required by CMS guidance implemented in 2023.

Observation billing requires the hospital outpatient POS (POS 22) rather than inpatient POS (POS 21), and uses the hospital E/M code series with specific documentation requirements distinct from inpatient billing. PMEx applies CMS Two-Midnight Rule criteria to determine the correct admission status for every hospital encounter routing to inpatient Part A billing when documentation supports a reasonable expectation of two-midnight stay, and observation billing with correct POS and code set when it does not.

Yes. PCM (99424/99425) is a 2022 CMS program for patients with a single high-complexity chronic condition requiring substantial ongoing physician management distinct from CCM, which covers patients with multiple conditions. PMEx identifies qualifying patients (CKD, uncontrolled diabetes, advanced heart failure, COPD requiring specialist-level management), implements PCM documentation, tracks monthly time, and bills the appropriate code tier adding $60 to $100 per qualifying patient per month in new revenue.

Prolonged services add-on codes (99417 for outpatient visits, G2212 for Medicare outpatient visits) can be billed when a visit exceeds the typical time threshold for a level 5 E/M by 15 minutes or more, provided total physician time is documented in the clinical note. PMEx identifies prolonged service visits through time documentation review and applies the correct add-on code capturing $95 to $135 of additional revenue per qualifying encounter. Most internal medicine practices have qualifying prolonged visits every day and never bill the add-on.

Yes. Advance care planning (99497 for the first 30 minutes, 99498 for additional 30-minute increments) is a Medicare-covered benefit for discussions about end-of-life care preferences code of care, resuscitation preferences, advance directives. PMEx identifies qualifying encounters from clinical documentation and bills ACP codes alongside the visit E/M adding $80 to $140 per qualifying encounter. Most internal medicine practices perform these discussions regularly and never capture the billing.

Critical care billing (99291 for the first 30 to 74 minutes, 99292 for each additional 30 minutes) requires documentation of a critical illness or injury and physician presence providing direct care with strict time requirements documented separately from procedure time. PMEx ensures critical care documentation meets CMS standards, applies the correct time-based code tiers, and captures the significantly higher reimbursement for qualifying encounters. Critical care pays $604 per first hour versus $112 for a standard hospital subsequent care visit.
